question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man with hypertension and well-controlled type 2 diabetes was brought to the emergency department by his spouse late this afternoon because his right lower limb had grown noticeably larger from groin to ankle over the past 36 hours. One week earlier he developed a febrile viral gastroenteritis that left him exhausted and he subsequently remained in bed except for brief bathroom trips; the step counter on his watch recorded fewer than 300 steps per day for four consecutive days, and he did not leave the house during that period. Two days ago his gastrointestinal symptoms abated, yet when he attempted to walk to the kitchen yesterday morning he felt a diffuse heaviness of the entire right leg that progressed throughout the day, forcing him to use the bannister when climbing the stairs to his bedroom. He denies any blunt trauma, twisting injury, insect bite, new medication, recent vaccination, or prolonged automobile or air travel. He has never experienced a clot in his legs or lungs, has no known thrombophilia, and is not taking anticoagulants or hormone preparations. His last operative procedure was an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy eleven months ago; there have been no invasive interventions, catheterizations, or orthopedic devices applied to the lower extremities since that time. He walks unassisted when well and has no history of stroke, spinal cord injury, limb weakness, or casting. Family history is negative for venous thromboembolism before the age of fifty, and he quit smoking fifteen years ago after a twenty-pack-year exposure. Review of systems today is negative for chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, fever, chills, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. On arrival—prior to administration of any medication—vital signs were temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. He appeared alert, oriented, and mildly uncomfortable when shifting his weight. Cardiac examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. Abdomen was soft with well-healed periumbilical scars and no tenderness or organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities showed a striking global enlargement of the right limb: circumference measured at mid-thigh was 54 cm on the right versus 50 cm on the left, at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity 38.4 cm on the right and 37.0 cm on the left—a disparity of 1.4 cm—and around the ankle 30 cm versus 28 cm. The skin over the swollen leg was slightly taut and warm but retained normal coloration without erythema or brawny hyperpigmentation. A conspicuous lattice of bluish, straight superficial channels coursed obliquely across the medial thigh and posterior calf and became more prominent when the limb dangled off the stretcher for several seconds; no serpiginous varicosities were present elsewhere. There was a generalized ache when the calf and posterior thigh were compressed, yet no discrete cord or focal point of maximal tenderness could be identified along the presumed deep venous paths. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was intact distally, and motor testing revealed 5/5 strength in ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, and knee extension bilaterally. Distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2+ and symmetric, and capillary refill of all toes was brisk. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy, knee effusion, or hip tenderness. The contralateral limb and both upper extremities were of normal size. Point-of-care laboratories obtained before any therapy showed hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, platelet count 245 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, and an INR of 1.0 with activated partial thromboplastin time 28 seconds. Plain radiographs of the femur and tibia demonstrated only soft-tissue prominence without fracture or gas. The absence of local skin inflammation, musculoskeletal injury, or lymphatic obstruction, combined with the full-length unilateral swelling, recent prolonged recumbency exceeding three days, conspicuous collateral superficial channels, and lack of a comparable prior event, makes an occlusion within the deep venous circulation the most plausible current explanation, and duplex ultrasonography of the entire right leg has been ordered to confirm the suspected pathology before anticoagulation is considered.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Wells DVT score: add 1 for each positive criterion and subtract 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
• Bedridden for at least 3 days or recent major surgery: +1 for 4 days of bed rest. The surgery 11 months ago does not qualify.
• Entire leg swollen: +1 for swelling from groin to ankle.
• Nonvaricose collateral superficial veins: +1 for the prominent straight superficial channels.
• Calf circumference difference ≥3 cm: 0; the difference at the specified site is only 38.4 − 37.0 = 1.4 cm.
• Localized deep venous tenderness: 0; the discomfort is diffuse.
• Active cancer, paralysis/paresis or cast immobilization, documented unilateral pitting edema, and previous DVT: 0 each.
• Alternative diagnosis at least as likely: no, so no deduction.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
